findings.title: Test of feature-model resolution mocks only one provider id
findings.rationale: The test exercises `resolveFeatureModel` (used in the conventions scan). Per the repo’s house rule, a test that goes through that code path must register `MockLLMProvider` under **all** three provider ids (`openai`, `anthropic`, `openrouter`) so that a future swap of the default provider id does not silently cause the test to call a real, paid API. The current registration under only `openrouter` violates that rule, exactly as warned in `server/INSIGHTS.md:26`. This bypass is invisible in CI but will break when the default changes, exactly the bug that was fixed in commit `f5323f7`.

findings.title: Mock registered under only one provider ID, not all three
findings.rationale: The test registers `MockLLMProvider` only under the `openrouter` provider id, but `resolveFeatureModel` can resolve the model from any of the three configured providers (`openai`, `anthropic`, `openrouter`). If the registry default changes to a provider that is not mocked (e.g., `openai`), the test will hit a real, paid API. This pattern is explicitly warned against in the repo’s test-quality house rules (see `conventions.it.test.ts:85-90` for the correct pattern).

findings.title: MockLLMProvider registered only under one provider ID instead of all three
findings.rationale: The integration test builds the app with an `overrides.llm` that registers `MockLLMProvider` only under `openrouter`. The conventions extraction resolves its model through `resolveFeatureModel`, which can fall back to the registry default for any of the three provider IDs (`openai`, `anthropic`, `openrouter`). When the registry default changes (as it has before, see INSIGHTS.md:26), the under‑mocked provider will cause the test to call a real, paid API instead of the mock, making the test both flaky and potentially expensive. The repository’s established pattern (conventions.it.test.ts:85‑90) registers the mock under all three IDs to guard against this. This is a **WARNING** per the test‑quality house rule, as it introduces a real flake source and a risk of unintended API calls.

findings.title: Hardcoded Production Secret in Source Code
findings.rationale: Hardcoded secret 'kluczProdukcyjny' directly in source code violates security best practices. Such secrets are easy to miss in code reviews and may be exposed in version control or leaked unintentionally.

findings.title: Test silently passes when Docker is unavailable
findings.rationale: The entire test suite and the single `it` block return early when Docker is unavailable (`beforeAll` returns on line 16, `it` returns on line 21). This means the test always passes — even if Postgres is never started — and no assertion is ever evaluated. A developer without Docker sees green tests and gains false confidence that the aggregation is correct. In CI with Docker, this is fine, but the test should signal its skip explicitly.

findings.title: Test does not verify aggregation is per-PR
findings.rationale: The test only inserts runs for a single PR and asserts a global sum. The feature intent is 'per-repo cost total', which almost certainly groups by `pr_id` (or `pull_request_id`). Without inserting a second PR and verifying that its sum is independent (e.g. another PR with 0.05 sums to 0.05, not 0.08), the test does not prove the GROUP BY clause works — a regression that merged costs across PRs would pass this test.

findings.title: Test assertion contradicts column nullability
findings.rationale: The column is defined as nullable without a default; inserting without a `retryCount` value stores `null` in the database. The test then asserts `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()`, which will always fail. This means the test does not validate the stated purpose (column round-trips) and cannot guard the described feature. A correct test would either insert a concrete value and check equality, or assert `toBeNull()` to demonstrate nullability.

findings.title: Test does not exercise GROUP BY — would not catch a missing or incorrect grouping clause
findings.rationale: The test filters on a single prId and checks the SUM result, but the production code (described as SELECT SUM(cost_usd) GROUP BY pr_id) computes per-repo totals by grouping multiple PRs.  This test never inserts a second PR or asserts that the sums are correctly partitioned, so a regression that removes or breaks the GROUP BY clause would still pass.  The gap is a correctness risk for the per-repo cost total feature.

matched_title: Test asserts non-null on unset nullable column — will always fail

findings.title: Test asserts non-null on unset nullable column — will always fail
findings.rationale: The test inserts an `agentRuns` row without setting `retryCount`, then asserts `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()`. Because the column is nullable and has no default, the inserted row will have `retryCount = null`. This assertion will always fail, making the test red and providing no value. The claimed purpose is to 'round-trip through a real insert/select', but the test never sets a value to verify round-trip. This is a critical flaw because the test is logically broken and cannot guard the intended behavior.

matched_title: Test assertion always fails: column is null when not set but assertion expects non-null

findings.title: Test assertion always fails: column is null when not set but assertion expects non-null
findings.rationale: The test inserts an agent run without providing a value for `retryCount`. Because the column is nullable and has no database default (`integer('retry_count')` without `default(...)` or `notNull()`), Postgres stores `NULL`. The assertion `expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()` on line 23 will therefore always fail. The test claims to verify the column round-trips, but as written it cannot pass, provides no meaningful coverage, and would break CI.

matched_title: Test asserts non-null for a nullable column with no default – will always fail

findings.title: Test asserts non-null for a nullable column with no default – will always fail
findings.rationale: The column `retry_count` is defined as a nullable integer without a default value. The insert on line 17 does not set `retryCount`, so the database stores NULL. The assertion on line 20 (`expect(row.retryCount).not.toBeNull()`) will always fail. The test therefore does not validate that the column round-trips correctly; it asserts the opposite of what the schema guarantees. This test would block the PR on every run, providing no meaningful coverage of the production change.

matched_title: No tests for SQL injection prevention in repository queries

findings.title: No tests for SQL injection prevention in repository queries
findings.rationale: The diff adds raw SQL with string interpolation (`sql.raw(...`${token}'...`) for `findByToken` and three other queries. No test exists that validates SQL injection is prevented (e.g., by using parameterized queries or escaping). If a token containing `' OR 1=1 --` were passed, the query would return unintended rows. The entire security of the token-as-capability authorization model depends on this, but the test suite contains zero tests for this code path.

findings.title: No tests for shell injection prevention when exporting or snapshotting
findings.rationale: `execSync` is called with string interpolation of `digestId` (line 75) and `label` (line 109). Neither value is validated or escaped. A digest ID containing `; rm -rf /` would execute arbitrary shell commands. No test verifies that the shell invocation is safe. This is a CRITICAL gap because the vulnerability would be permanently exploitable in production without any test catching it.

findings.title: No tests for the token-authorization model or password gate
findings.rationale: The `getSharedDigest` method is the public read path. It uses the token as the sole authorization. No test exists that verifies: (a) a valid token returns the correct digest, (b) a missing/expired token throws `NotFoundError`, (c) a token with a password returns the digest only if the password is verified (currently the password is stored but never checked in the public route — see line 44-51, no password check). The code currently accepts any token without requiring the password hash to match, meaning the optional password feature is completely untested and likely broken. This is a CRITICAL authorization gap.

findings.title: No tests for error handling in unfurl method
findings.rationale: `unfurl` calls `fetch(url)` and `res.text()` without any error handling for network failures, non-200 responses, or non-text content (e.g., binary files, giant pages). The method assumes success. No test covers these error branches. A fetch failure would throw an unhandled promise rejection, likely returning a 500 to the client.

findings.title: No tests for snapshotExports error paths
findings.rationale: `snapshotExports` performs two operations (shell command then API call), each able to fail independently. The code only catches API failure (throw `AppError`), but shell failure would throw a generic error. No test validates that a failed `execSync` is handled gracefully (e.g., does not leave partial state) or that a slow/unresponsive maintenance API is timed out.
